variants.headline: Looking back without polishing the past
variants.sub: The founding years deserve reflection without an invented golden age.
variants.body:
Looking back at the founding years of {colony} is an invitation to think about beginnings. It is also an invitation to a familiar mistake: making the past conveniently agree with whatever one wants to argue about the present.

A founding is a beginning, not a complete answer to every question that follows. The colony's origin deserves attention without being turned into a claim that its later choices were already settled. Memory should open a discussion about purpose, rather than close it with an invented account of unanimous intention.

Consider the standard a useful retrospective ought to meet. It should distinguish an attachment to the beginning from a claim to know every person's hopes. It should allow the present to ask questions of the past, without asking the past to supply a flattering verdict on the present writer's politics.

The gazette distinguishes reflection from a historical entry. This column records no additional episode or attribution from the founding years. Its subject is the care with which a common beginning should be considered in the colony's public life.

variants.headline: The founding years and the uses of memory
variants.sub: The founding years deserve reflection without an invented golden age.
variants.body:
The founding years can become a very comfortable place for an argument to hide. Everyone is invited to admire the beginning; the difficult question is what that admiration asks of life in {colony} now. A retrospective should have room for the question.

There is a difference between honouring a common undertaking and announcing what every founder would have wanted. The first can be a serious political and human act. The second requires knowledge a pleasant phrase cannot supply. A newspaper should not invent a consensus merely because it would make the ending more satisfying.

Think of the colony's beginning as a reason to examine responsibility. What does it mean to continue a place rather than simply praise its origin? That is an opinion worth discussing, and it needs neither a fabricated hardship nor a fictional speech to make it matter.

variants.headline: A beginning is not a finished argument
variants.sub: The founding years deserve reflection without an invented golden age.
variants.body:
A beginning attracts a story. In looking back at the founding years of {colony}, the useful discipline is to remember that a good story is not entitled to add facts merely because they feel suitable to the occasion.

The past can be admired without being made perfect. It can be questioned without being dismissed. Those are judgments about how to remember, not claims about a particular decision or a named person's purpose. A retrospective becomes more useful when it leaves room for that distinction.

The question for readers is what a founding should mean to the work of living together. Pride may be part of the answer. Responsibility should be part of it too. A colony cannot live entirely inside the account of how it began; the beginning matters partly because there is a present in which to consider it.

variants.headline: Remembering why a colony begins
variants.sub: The founding years deserve reflection without an invented golden age.
variants.body:
What do we ask of the founding years when we look back? Sometimes the question is about belonging. Sometimes it is about purpose. The newspaper's task is to allow those questions without filling the past with people and episodes it has not established.

A colony's origin can provide a language of common effort. It should not become an instruction to agree about every later choice. People can value a beginning while arguing seriously about the obligations that follow from it. The disagreement need not make the attachment less real.

This retrospective therefore proposes a modest standard for memory: use it to think, rather than to avoid thinking. The founding of {colony} deserves more than a polished phrase placed beyond examination. It deserves the attention we give to something whose meaning can still require an honest conversation among the people who inherit it.
